speechtext:

speechtext:

POSSIBILITY OF OPENING AND ADJOURNING SESSIONS AT FIXED DATES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion on a very important matter.
Considering that once more this session is running the risk of being extended into the middle of summer; that it would be greatly advantageous for all Canadians if sessions of Parliament were held at fixed periods of time; and that most parliamentarians, if not all, approve this idea, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin):
That the House instruct the Committee on Procedure and Organization to hold a meeting as soon as possible to consider the advisability of holding sessions of Parliament at fixed periods of time in the future and also to set dates for holidays and other statutory holidays to allow parliamentarians to be with their families during holidays and thus have a better organized life.

with respect to the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, or a northern pipeline, which the government House leader, who really missed his true calling as an illusionist, has dangled before us without handing us anything of substance with respect to the matter. In view of the statement by the House leader on Friday that all relevant reports must be taken into account, would the Prime Minister assure the House that his House leader meant what he said and that parliament must be allowed to debate all relevant reports, including the Lysyk report, before a government decision is taken?

subtopic: NORTHERN PIPELINE-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF DEBATE ON ALL RELEVANT REPORTS PRIOR TO DECISION

In view of the commitment which has now been given, I have a supplementary question. There was a proposition put forward under Standing Order 43 by the Leader of the Opposition in which he gave a detailed proposal for the examination of the evidence by a special committee which would serve as collator and distiller of the various inquiries which have been made, drawing conclusions from the totality of the evidence and bringing its findings before the whole House. FREIGHT RATES-POSSIBILITY OF SET RATE FOR PAYMENTS TO FLOUR MILLERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport arising out of answers which he gave to questions yesterday. In response to a question that I put to him regarding freight rates the minister replied that the government is meeting the problem of stop-off charges in eastern Canada by lowering the stop-off charges in western Canada and supporting the difference by paying funds directly to the flour millers. Is it the intention of the minister to maintain a set rate for flour millers, which at the moment I believe is 7 cents per hundred? In the meantime other charges have gone up, making the total 18 cents, and the millers are footing another 11 cents a hundred. Is it the minister's policy that where he reimburses a miller or a rapeseed crusher, the amount shall remain at that set rate regardless of what happens to other charges or freight rates?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: FREIGHT RATES-POSSIBILITY OF SET RATE FOR PAYMENTS TO FLOUR MILLERS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member's facts are wrong. The government payment has gone up to 15 cents, which at the present time as I understand it, is the most recent differential between the eastern stop-off charge and the western stop-off charge. We have not assured the millers that we can continue tracking the difference in rate in this fashion because of problems of financial restraint, but up to this point we have done so.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the minister indicated that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House have been reluctant to say, anywhere but in the west, what they mean by equity. We have been advocating a system of equalized and/or subsidized freight rates since about 1933 all over Canada, and I would like to ask the minister if it is going to be his policy upon termination- because he says he wants in the long run to arrive at a better system than the one he is presently stuck with-to have as a long range policy a system of equalizing or subsidizing freight rates for the regions of Canada which are affected because of distance; for example, the Atlantic provinces and western Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Where very specific developmental purposes can be served by lower freight rates, we have recognized the usefulness of them, as we did in our recent discussions with the Atlantic provinces and in the agreement to aim freight assistance specifically at products where that leads to Atlantic development. I cannot, however, share the hon. member's view-which I understand his party can adopt easily-that somehow there is some magic and beautiful solution in transferring from the person who ships goods to the taxpayer the cost of freight. The fact is that those costs do not go away, no matter how much the hon. member

May 18, 1977

might like to dream and pretend that they do. They are still borne by the taxpayer, and in addition, because they are hidden and not taken into account in our total domestic production pattern, they lead to increases in cost and lower productivity in Canada, which is something we must attack very vigorously indeed.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, that is the kind of talk we have been getting since 1880.
Oh, oh!

I would like to ask the minister if the government intends to fly not just in the face of what 1 say or what the NDP says but also in the face of what many organizations, and most recently the Hall Commission, have said? In terms of the use of instruments like the statutory grain rates applying to the finished products, whether it be grain or other kinds of products, does the minister intend to ignore the recommendations of the Hall Commission and continue with the 1890 concept he still embraces?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
The hon. member earlier said 1880, and I felt that with another three years and the 100th anniversary of hearing it, he might understand what is involved. 1 did indicate the other day my concern about this particular freight rate issue. I have said repeatedly that I do not want that in any way to detract from the Hall Commission, which was set up very specifically to do a major job for western Canada and which I played a part in setting up. The job it has done has been excellent, and we will be implementing a great number of the proposals of the Hall Commission.
In this particular case I did not point out-and I would like the hon. member to register this-that if there is a suggestion that an artificially low rate well below cost be allowed for the movement of meat, I presume even the hon. member would not suggest that this could be done only for western Canada. It would have to apply all across the country, and I simply say to the hon. member that unlike his leader and the Leader of the Opposition, it may be worthwhile to take a statement like that in a report and calculate what it would cost even before he determines that he would want that cost transferred to the taxpayer. At the very least he should know what it costs and what the economic implications of transferring this cost to the taxpayer are before he decides to support it.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
That this House notes with alarm the government's continuing inability to provide Canadians with an efficient postal service, its obsession with secrecy, its illegal use of orders in council to set postal rates, and its chronic ineptness in the field of collective bargaining and industrial relations, and recommends that the operations of the Post Office Department be referred to a special joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during the past few weeks there have been at least three occasions on which Post Office affairs have been discussed both within this House and by the Committee on Transport and Communications. On each occasion the members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition have become increasingly concerned by a drift toward a situation which can only result in final confrontation and complete breakdown in the postal service. It is for this reason we are taking the opportunity today to bring a motion before the House in a conscientious endeavour to get some action before the point of no return is passed.
As I came into the House today I received a press release from the Canadian Union of Postal Workers expressing the same kind of alarm. Coincidentally, I do not know whether some telepathy is involved, but it indicates that the people most concerned with providing a postal service have come to the same conclusion as the members of the opposition. I have been receiving a growing volume of complaints about slow delivery, damaged letters and parcels, lost mail and rapid increases in rates for all postal services, and at the same time decline in service. My mail, when the mail does get through, also includes a growing number of complaints from postal employees indicating a continuing decline in morale. A recent letter from a long-time postal officer concluded with these words, and I can assure the House that this is not an exceptional case:
I actually see a dying Post Office now. I notice more evidence of it every day. I am saddened by it all. I no longer support the policies of the union. They are

May 18, 1977
Post Office
partly responsible for some of the problems; however, only a small part as most of their foolishness was allowed and seldom even understood by the management negotiations. As an example, the hiring of casuals was a concession that should not have been discontinued; but instead partly discontinued. It should have been pegged to the rate of absenteeism, sick leave, annual and special leave, and maintained at that level.
The disillusionment expressed by this experienced postal worker summarizes what has happened to Canada's Post Office during the past nine years. The high morale that used to characterize the postal service has given way to a growing sense of frustration. The Postmaster General (Mr. Blais), in his remarks to the third Postal User's Conference held in Toronto on November 2, 1976, expressed the same sense of futility. He declared that any further strike action by the CUPW would destroy the postal service. It is reflected, too, in the numerous studies undertaken by the Post Office in attempting to cure the growing malaise, the phrase the former postmaster general, Bryce Mackasey, used to use frequently.
Altogether, some 15 studies have been undertaken. Because they have been highly critical of current trends in Post Office management, administration and labour relations, successive postmasters general have endeavoured to keep a shroud of secrecy around them, thereby denying members of parliament opportunity to engage in informed discussion on ways and means to improve the postal service.
All major industrial countries have been passing through difficulties similar to Canada in upgrading their postal services to meet the demand for modern communications. Denied access to Canadian studies, members of the Conservative party's caucus committee on postal affairs visited the United States and the United Kingdom in search of answers to the Canadian postal dilemma. In both countries we found a refreshing openness and desire to share their problems and experience with us. Just the other day I received volume 1, dated April, 1977, of the report of the commission on postal service from the United States government. In the foreword to the President and Congress of the United States the purpose of the commission is stated briefly thus:
The commission was established to identify and study problems facing the United States postal service and to recommend actions to resolve these problems.
The British are completing a similar study known as the Carter commission report. Our Conservative caucus committee has received the assurance that we will receive a copy as soon as it is off the press. In light of the openness of the United States and British governments, the paranoic secretiveness of the Canadian government is incomprehensible when we view the situation that faces us. This paranoid attitude on the part of the government has influenced and poisoned all relationships in the Canadian postal service. Back in 1969, when Eric Kierans was postmaster general, the decision was taken to move Canada's postal service into the twentieth century by a program of mechanization and automation. Without any prior consultation with the postal unions, the plan was thrown at them as a fait accompli. This was the beginning of the breakdown in labour-management relations which has resulted today in a situation where the CUPW is still boycotting the
postal code, an innovation which is essential to the success of the automation program.
In his speech to the Postal Users' Conference in Toronto last fall, the Postmaster General referred to yet another study that has just been completed by the Post Office. It was conducted by a sociologist from the University of Alberta and took the form of video-taped interviews with employees. Here is a summary of some of the complaints given by the PMG on page 9 of his speech:
Management never consults us. They never ask for our "input". They never ask how we feel or think. They never get down to the plant floor and find out what's going on. They bring in machines and they tell us how they work, but they don't say how they affect our future.
Some complained about shift work, some about heat and noise. But many more said they were treated either like army recruits or children. Surprisingly, few complain about the computerized machinery. Morale has dropped among those who do not work machines: manual sorters, mail handlers, people in transportation-older, long-time employees who are the backbone of the Post Office. They see mechanization eroding their jobs, depreciating their skills. They think we lavish too much attention and money on machines.
Too much haste in proceeding toward mechanization has produced a situation in Toronto, which processes 45 per cent of all the mail originating in Canada, that we have outlined in this House in questions in recent days and has been referred to by the Postmaster General as a temporary aberration. Mail is being delayed up to ten days, many letters lost, some destroyed by the sorting machinery, and only 35 per cent being sorted by the mechanization process. This results in the necessity of expensive double-banking, with the new, automated machines having to be backed up by a large staff of manual sorters.
Enough has been said to underline the problem, and other speakers will be raising other matters. Now we must move toward solutions. The British and American experience is enlightening in this respect. Both countries have moved away from direct government control to a Crown corporation set up in the United Kingdom and a semi-private organization in the United States. Both countries were faced with strikes in the initial stages of transition. In the U.K. management made the same mistake that has been made in Canada: mechanization was thrown at the union without prior consultation. The United Postal Workers struck and refused to go back to work until such time as they had been thoroughly consulted on the whole process of mechanization and automation.
Management declared a one-year moratorium on the implementation of the plan. Union representatives were brought directly into the planning process. They came up with some of the best ideas. They now sit on the board of directors of the Post Office with management. I talked with Norman Stagg, the deputy general secretary of the Union of Postal Workers of Great Britain, and was amazed to hear him talk of members of the Union of Postal Workers as part of the Post Office family dedicated to operating the best postal service possible. Oh, that we could have this situation in the Canadian Post Office!

May 18, 1977

They view mechanization and automation as the long-term solution provided the workers are closely involved in the formulation-and this is important-as well as the implementation stage and share the benefits of mechanization. The position of machine coder has become an elite position in mechanized postal plants, and we had the opportunity to see old-time employees displaying excellent morale as they vied one with another for speed and accuracy with coding machines.
At the present time, plans are afoot to introduce full-scale industrial democracy into the British postal plants. Incidentally, they are coming on stream at a much slower pace than the impulsive pace which has been adopted in Canada, with 18 offices out of a planned 80 on stream, and installations are proceeding at the rate of ten a year. In the United States the experience has been similar. They, too, had a strike in the early stages, even though the right to strike is not given to employees in essential services. Now consultation has been introduced in all areas of the United States postal service and at all levels. Training programs have been established for both management and labour.
As is the case in Britain, supervisors and shop stewards attend courses together to be trained in modern industrial relations skills and sensitized to problems of human relations on the plant floor. Local grievances are dealt with at the local level, thereby avoiding the huge backlog of unsettled grievances, many of them trivial and avoidable, which is poisoning the spirit of good, human relations in Canada's mechanized postal plants. It is interesting to note that the commission which reported recently to the President and Congress included representatives from both the postal workers and letter carriers union in its membership.
During the next few weeks, the Canada Post Office is faced with critical negotiations for new contracts with all its employees. The Canadian Union of Postal Workers, which represents most inside workers, have already expressed their militancy by making 250 new proposals for a one-year agreement, and stating, "We're ready to strike again if we have to. It's second nature to us."
In committee meetings last week, the Postmaster General emphasized that management and labour were still on a collision confrontation course. He pointed out that a no cooperation and fraternization clause is written into the constitution of the union. He said the same in his speech last fall:
All signs appear to me to point to a breakdown in communications. Each party has been unable to accept the other for what they are. Labels have been used "militaristic", "dictatorial", "Maoists", "separatist" when they failed to accept the reality. Propaganda in its World War II sense has been used on both sides.
This was the situation over which the former postmaster general, Bryce Mackasey, stumbled in his attempts to solve the problems in the Post Office. Mr. Mackasey's growing disillu-sionments are outlined in a series of speeches published by the Post Office, so they must have considered them important, under the revealing title "What's Behind the Lemming Urge"?
Post Office
In other words, we were all going over the cliff together. His closing sentence is most illuminating in light of what I have outlined today, and I quote:
We're moving beyond ideology; we're responding to necessity. Our choice, as Buchminster Fuller says, is between Utopia and oblivion.
Everyone is agreed that the strike weapon is not the solution. This is pointed out in CUPW's press release today. The workers in the University of Alberta study state that they were gratified and encouraged to be consulted. They said they would like to take pride in their work; they would like the satisfaction of doing their best; they would like to give service. They said, "If management were on our side, we'd be on theirs". The Postmaster General, too, has stated:
-with every stoppage of work, the Post Office Department loses more business to private couriers, teleprinters networks, computerized message systems and the long distance telephone. We have to stop the drain or we'll end up like the States, where the cost of service pushes up rates as mail volume goes down, and then volume goes down because mailing rates go up.
He further quoted Jack Jones, the moderate leader of Britain's largest trade union, when he said recently, "What's the use of a beautiful wage agreement if the firm goes bust five days later"? The dialogue of the deaf must cease. Management has already achieved a good relationship with the Letter Carriers Union of Canada. It must now come to grips with the Canadian Union of Postal Workers. The leaders of the union want to be heard and want to be involved. We believe that our motion offers the only solution, and we trust that the government will support it.
May I make a further motion, or suggestion, in view of its timeliness, that the press release and the attached excerpts from the Uberig report, which is a significant report by the assistant deputy minister for the Post Office, be appended to Hansard today as part of the record?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was just about to begin my remarks when the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) rose on this question. I am glad he did. It is one of the few opportunities we have to stand in this House and talk about the Post Office and the way it is managed. I think the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) should be complimented for bringing forward this motion.
Having said that, the motion that has been put is the real crux of the problem. Studies have been made about the management of the Post Office, but there sits the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) saying "No" to providing parliament and the public with the facts of the situation. This whole matter of the secrecy that operates within the Post Office has been one of the stumbling blocks to any kind of attempt to bring order to it. The Postmaster General cannot claim that the Post Office is a Crown corporation and therefore we cannot interfere. Neither can he claim that it is an entity separate to itself. It is not. The Post Office Department is run by the Postmaster General, and he is responsible to parliament for the postal service in this country. The Post Office Act states that the Postmaster General shall administer, superintend and manage the Post Office, so he cannot hide behind the faqade of a Crown corporation or secret documents.
We want to know how the postal service is being administered. There are complaints from one end of the country to the other from people who are supposed to receive the benefit of an extensive service. There are also complaints from the people who sort the mail and deliver it, with respect to the way the Post Office is run. The Postmaster General has avoided providing parliament with the facts about the Post Office. That is a travesty of the purpose of parliament. It is an example of what happens when departments are not held accountable to the people. This minister, like the Post Office, tends to be accountable to no one.
The Postmaster General always has the wisecrack; he thinks this is a great big joke. Mr. Speaker, that is symptomatic of what is wrong with the Post Office. Middle management and top management bureaucrats take the example of the Postmaster General. Six months ago he was saying there was going to be a strike in the Post Office. In January of this year we asked him to open negotiations early in order to avoid problems which tend to become compressed, and sometimes we find ourselves crushed by them when trying to meet a deadline for a strike. He said the rules and regulations did not permit that. Yet out in Vancouver he was smiling like a Cheshire cat and telling us to be ready for a strike. This goes to show the minister's ineptitude when it comes to collective bargaining and industrial relations. So much for the Postmaster General and the incompetence with which he has handled the postal service, Mr. Speaker.
May 18, 1977

From my experience with the Post Office, 1 believe the problem lies with middle management. I do not think they have the basic concept of how to direct the work force. They seem to treat the work force in a very childish fashion, talking down to them. They have no idea of how to direct the work force in a meaningful way, with creativity, patience and imagination. Many of the problems which occur in the Post Office seem to revolve around the question of interpersonal relationships between those who are supposed to carry out instructions and those who are supposed to give direction.
A previous deputy postmaster general, Mr. Mackay, attempted to do two things, to decentralize the Post Office operations and to introduce technological change. This has been noted from time immemorial. Mr. Justice Freedman talked about the effect of technological change on the work force of the railways and the right of the work force to ensure that it did not suffer adverse effects from it. He held that there should be some method of retraining or reclassifying the work force to make sure that the effects of technological change did not fall heavily on them. One would assume that would be uppermost in the mind of management.
The Post Office work force did not object to technological change. They were concerned about the effects it might have and wanted to cushion them as much as possible. Those are legitimate concerns, Mr. Speaker. Anybody who has a heart, some common sense and ingenuity with respect to management would recognize that the problem has to be dealt with. It was not dealt with, and as a result we had a strike over the question of technological change.
Sad to say, and to the lasting disgrace of the Post Office, they began to engage in a propaganda fight with the postal union, attempting to get a scapegoat and to blame the workers for the problems in the Post Office which resulted in the strike. Everyone pointed the finger at those who were most visible- the people carrying the picket posters. It was the leadership of the union which had to speak out on behalf of the membership. Time and again the minister said that a technological change clause, and all sorts of things, would be included in the collective agreement. Finally, it was done. Now the problem is with the way it is interpreted. The workers are constantly finding great frustration in dealing with the whole question of interpretation. The Post Office management runs around the end of the clause and the 120-day notice provision. The problem of technological change is still a very serious one for the Post Office, and the Postmaster General seems incapable of handling this very delicate and human problem.
The other thing that Mr. Mackay attempted to do was decentralize the authority of the Post Office. This is pretty difficult when there is not sophisticated management and management seems incapable of exerting leadership and accepting responsibility for decentralization. So we had regional offices operating completely independent of the central administration.
Post Office
Local post offices were completely ignoring regional office instructions and doing only what they thought they should be doing and what they had always done. We also know-and this is not unknown to the workers, either-that often it became an old boy's club. Middle management brought its own kind into the group, and often this created problems because people who had no knowledge of the postal service got into positions of authority.
The hon. member for Brandon-Souris recommends in his motion a parliamentary committee made up of members of this House and members of the other place. I do not know what the other place could possibly have to say about the postal services in this country.

speechtext:
Yes, they have a lot of time to think. We know that, but the Canadian Union of Postal Workers raised a very legitimate point. The Union suggested that the postal service is a bone over which politicians fight. CUPW proposed a royal commission to look into the total operation of the Post Office in this country. To me, that is a common sense suggestion. Quite frankly and personally, I do not have much faith in commissions studying things, because the minister is responsible. The minister has the power, and all we need is a minister with a backbone instead of a wishbone. Then we could get things done and some changes could be made in the Post Office. Instead, we just fumble along. Be that as it may, CUPW has suggested a royal commission. It seems to me that an independent group could study the operation of the Post Office apart from political implications which would be involved with an interparliamentary committee.
What does the minister reply to that suggestion? That suggestion was made to him. Not long ago, before he came into this House, he was told that CUPW suggested this. What was his response? He said that he would be quite prepared to set up a royal commission provided CUPW would be prepared to suspend its collective bargaining until after the report of the royal commission. Well, postal workers do not have that kind of time. They do not have a decade. They have to meet the cost of living-and the minister knows that. Surely the minister should know that there cannot be tit-for-tat in this way. My 13-year old child could understand the mechanics of that.
This minister does not want a royal commission, in spite of the fact that he says he would welcome one. If he really wanted a royal commission to look into postal services, he would not suggest that a group of workers suspend the collective bargaining process while we go through this procedure. We have had royal commissions before. In 1966 we had the Montpetit royal commission. In 1969 we had "Blueprint for Change". Just recently we had yet another important report which was called "Canada Post, 1975".
All these reports said the same thing. They complained about the management of the Post Office; they complained about the paternalism of the Post Office and suggested possi-

May 18, 1977
Post Office
ble solutions. One possible solution suggested in the past was the creation of a Crown corporation to run the Post Office. But the government would not have any part of that. The postmaster general of that time wanted to run the Post Office himself. Perhaps if a Crown corporation had been set up, the postal workers would have come under the Canada Labour Code. Perhaps, then, the government would have had to stop hiding behind a complicated tangle of conflicting legislation which allowed it to stall, to hide from the issues and to attack the unionized workers of the Post Office. It was not the unionized postal workers who created the mess the Post Office is now in. It was the government of Canada and its management of the Post Office.
Perhaps I might be forgiven if I become a little bit political here. It seems to me that the only difference between the way this Liberal government runs the Post Office and the way a Tory government would run it is that hon. colleagues to my right would use all the power of government to strangle any complaints from workers in the Post Office.

I suspect that much of the middle and top management of the Post Office comes from the armed services. They are "spit and polish" people. That is not an army setting-and that is one of the problems. I do not quarrel often with colleagues to my right because I like to get along with people in this House and I do not like to raise their ire.

Are the government negotiators no longer taking the position that the union has to accept this wage package before negotiating other questions? ... Has the government advised the union that a return to work order is a prerequisite to continuing negotiations in good faith?
The only difference between the way the Post Office is run now and the way it would be run by the Tories is that under the Tories there would be total suppression of the workers in that particular work force. It seems that the solution the hon. member suggested, the setting up of a parliamentary-

speechtext:
There are solutions to these problems in the Post Office, and in the past they have been suggested by some postmasters general. However, those suggestions have died as postmasters general have moved in and out of office. In the last few years there have been about four or five postmasters general, and it seems to me that perhaps the government thinks a moving target is hard to hit.
In conclusion, let me read a paragraph from a letter sent on November 1, 1969, by Messrs. Kates, Peat, Marwick and Company to the Hon. E. W. Kierans, former minister of communications. Mr. Kierans also acted at one time as postmaster general. The letter said in part:
Fifteen studies were conducted over the past 12 months by task forces which were assembled by the Post Office and utilized the services of six consulting firms. From these studies emerged the overpowering conclusion that the Post Office, as a Crown corporation, could better fulfil its role in the future.

May 18, 1977

Later, the letter said that even if the Post Office were made a Crown corporation, imagination, patience and leadership would be necessary. We know this, Mr. Speaker, and the joint committee proposed by Conservative members on my right will not alter the situation. A royal commission ought to be established, as requested by the workers of the Post Office. The minister ought to concur in that suggestion, without demanding any quid pro quo, that is to say, without saying, "If you stop negotiating, we will set up a royal commission." I say to the government, "You are not dealing with children. These are grown-up individuals who have an interest in the way the Post Office is run and depend on the Post Office for their livelihood."
We are not talking about teenagers, 13-year olds or young children. We are talking about people who have as much interest in seeing the Post Office properly run, as the people of Canada have in receiving good Post Office service. I say to the Postmaster General, in closing, "Appoint the royal commission. Let us get on with the job, without all this fiddle-faddling around."

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words to the present debate. It is quite obvious that if the government changes a procedure without the House's permission, it goes beyond its rights. In that case, I do support the motion before us which points out the government's continuing inability to provide Canadians with an efficient postal service, its obsession with secrecy, and its illegal use of orders-in-council to set postal rates.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot merely talk about democracy, we must put it into practice. And each time we proceed by decrees, we are interfering with that very principle. However, it must be said to the defence of the minister that his department must display increased efficiency and, consequently, some measures have to be taken to do so. But it is not a reason to proceed without the assent of the House. It is quite obvious that a service that could have been not only efficient but profit-earning must undergo some modifications. We have no objection to that but we would like to know first what are the measures being considered. That is the very subject of this motion since the minister could answer us that he only wants to improve the postal service through these orders-in-council. But again that does not alter the fact that if things have to be changed in the Post Office to get better service we should ask the House to pass adequate legislation to achieve that goal. It is the proper way to proceed.
As a matter of fact, it is by getting used to small orders which are apparently harmless that in the end we come to pass monstrosities. We must understand that we should be careful to prevent this. Several years ago, the Canadian postal service was a service we had every reason in the world to be proud of but these last few years it has considerably degenerated to the point where I received yesterday an invitation for an important appointment on May 11. What happens? I checked and I have been told that the invitation was sent on May 1. This is not an isolated case; I often had the opportunity to notice undue
Post Office
delays in mail delivery. How did all this happen? All this happened actually and this is one thing which is mentioned in the motion: the chronic ineptness in the field of collective bargaining and industrial relations. The climate among postal workers has been such for several years that this affects their production considerably. And all Canadians had to bear the consequences of this situation.
Yesterday, to give another example, I went myself to take messages delivered by bus service. I noticed on the premises that the parcel delivery section of the bus service is almost as important as the parcel delivery service of the Post Office.
Some people have found out by themselves that they would be better off with private services such as those. Yet, Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, we already had in this country an adequate postal service of which we could be proud. Some changes should be made and I believe that the government should make an effort to tell what it intends to do, to create, for instance, within the postal service, a climate that is healthy, that is invigorating, that can make the postal service very efficient if not profitable, since people will be more ready to admit the non-profitability of such a service if it is efficient. But when we see the inefficiency of the service, it is difficult to swallow the fact that it is also non-profitable, especially when we can see the services of private companies, which are sometimes no more expensive and which provide quick and reliable service.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is essential that the minister, who seems very willing, because I think that he is doing a good job, realize that it would be his duty to heed the comments we are making today so that he may submit a plan which would show a truly sincere way to bring about the necessary changes within his department. He should therefore stop to administer the postal service by orders-in-council and to authorize rate increases under the pretext that it will make the service more efficient.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude my comments by speaking about one last point. I agree that if we are to keep pace with progress we cannot avoid making changes to replace human workers by machines. We all know that there is such a problem in the Post Office, but I would like to say that we shall never solve this problem if we do not study seriously the suggestions that my party has been making for many years. One day we shall have to decide that we must relate progress, the use of machines, automation and the workers. If the machine replaces man, it will have to be to the advantage of man so that he can continue to live with a sufficient income. And we know that the problem in the postal service is partly caused by this principle of automation. And I insist that we shall not find a solution to this problem of the Post Office because it encompasses all others.
This is an over-all, global problem. And I am sure I do not exaggerate when I say that part of the problems the Post Office and all other departments are faced with result from the government's systematic refusal to transform the basic

May 18, 1977
Post Office
economic system which is inflicted, yes, inflicted upon us, which explains why intelligent people who can reason and judge reasonably well cannot solve this problem, for when a service like the Post Office is equipped with machines which can do in a few minutes what hundreds of people would require days to perform, one ends up with the following dilemma: what to do with all these employees?
If intelligent men are not able yet to find an answer there is certainly something wrong and it is the result of a systematic refusal to consider appropriate answers, particularly when we make every effort to suggest valid suggestions and God knows that the former leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada, Mr. Real Caouette, tried during more than 30 years to make people understand that basic principle: Let us not reject progress. If we build machines able to replace men, let us replace men by those machines. Let us not be stupid and let us find the means to give an income to workers and this is why we should change completely our wrong conception of work. We should get to the point where we shall distribute to everyone, without exception, a minimum income that will allow our citizens to live a decent and honest living.
This is the answer to all kinds of problems, particularly in the Post Office department where conflicts have been caused by labour problems and collective bargaining. For 35 years we have been saying in this House that this should be changed because the worst could happen. We wait for a catastrophe to react. Mr. Speaker, we are looking for trouble and we should avoid it.
I say to the minister that he should think not only of his problem with postal workers but also that he will solve that problem by considering the global answers we suggest to deal with general problems faced by workers. Any individual is entitled to a decent income and it is even more true if mechanization can give it to him. We do not need to give money to the machine. It does not need a purchasing power. If a machine replaces hundreds of men why should we not distribute that income to them? It is simple, Mr. Speaker. I am convinced that the minister will understand this and that, being a man of good will, someday he will study social credit to apply our solutions in his department in order to deal with all postal problems.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to thank the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) for his kindness to me. I was hoping that someone this afternoon might recognize the efficiency I have brought into the department over which I am presiding. So I thank him very much. Then not only do I recognize that the Social Credit Party of Canada holds a monopoly on a principle concerning the industrialization of the Post Office, but I also want to say that I approve that principle which I have largely supported since taking over at the Post Office. As the hon. member for Champlain is no doubt aware, there is in the collective agreement currently under negotiation a guarantee that no employee will lose his job nor suffer any income loss because of mechanization. Indeed, we have taken all kinds of measures
to make sure that Post Office employees will not bear the brunt of technological changes.
I would also like to recognize during the next round of collective bargaining the increased productivity resulting from such mechanization. This is a management principle, both very modern and very fair, and I totally agree that it should apply here.
I would also agree that there were problems from the outset with mail delivery. More recent problems are due to the transfer from manual to mechanical sorting, especially in the Toronto area. I have no doubt that the examples of slow delivery brought forward by the hon. member for Champlain involved that aberration in the Toronto area. But I would like to ask him to keep a close eye on his mail in the future, and I shall soon send a letter to his secretary asking to be informed of any undue and abnormal delay. Because we try to correct problems that may arise, we have established a quality evaluation system aimed directly at establishing links across the country and ensuring that the mail will be delivered within the predetermined time. If that deadline is not honoured, I would like to be informed so that we can review the situation. The hon. member for Champlain will no doubt agree that with a 60,000 labour force, of which nearly 20,000 are inside workers sorting the mail or supervising sorting machines, errors will be made. But we want to eliminate them.
It must also be remembered that the Post Office has more than 8,700 contracts with trucking firms moving the mail. Clearly, there may be shortcomings in that system. But I would like the hon. member for Champlain to agree that the system now being implemented is efficient, although it needs constant supervision, and that as a user of the mail service the hon. member is just as much part of that supervision as the people within the department.

Turning, now, from the very constructive remarks by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) to those of another quality and character, of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), I would first like to cite that although the hon. member for Nickel Belt made a great to-do about not answering questions, I did not see his puss at any time in the committee on transportation.
I understand he had to attend another committee. I am not speaking of that. We held two very full meetings, as the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) indicated, before the transport committee, and the hon. member for Nickel Belt was nowhere to be seen. There is also the comment he made that I did not have the sensitivity to resolve human problems within the Post Office. Mr. Speaker, I think I have a great deal of sensitivity to be able to stand here and listen to some of the burbling that was bandied about by the hon. member for Nickel Belt.
First of all, when asked this afternoon by reporters about a telegram I had just received from the president of CUPW, my reaction was to tell them that I did not think it was a bona fide

May 18, 1977

offer. The hon. member knows that the unions will be sitting with Post Office representatives tomorrow to begin negotiations on a new collective agreement. Hon. members know it is a constant practice of that union to engage in confrontation tactics. They know the union has taken a militant stand. It is a legitimate one, and I do not object to it. But I say the proposal this morning is one of two things: a move to upstage the hon. member for Brandon-Souris-and I do not think that at all- or an attempt to soften up the management of the Post Office in preparation for the negotiations.
Had it been otherwise, they would have indicated their seriousness in suggesting a royal commission by recognizing the consequences, namely, that while there is such a commission in being the Post Office ought to operate in a normal state, or in a state as near as possible to normal, and that by continuing the negotiations, we are now faced, once again, with a very confrontative situation. Any work which the royal commission might do would be frustrated at the outset. I doubt very much that one could get a royal commission operating at a time when negotiations were being conducted.
Again, when I was chastised by the hon. member for Nickel Belt as being insensitive to labour relations, I called to his attention the fact that one of the unions with which we are dealing, namely, the LCUC, has really come across as far as we have gone across to them. We have met, now, in 11 sessions, as I indicated to the committee, and the hon. member for Nickel Belt would have known this had he attended. We have had very successful results from these sessions. What disappoints me is that CUPW are not only taking a confrontative stand vis-a-vis the Post Office, but are now taking a confrontative stand vis-a-vis the letter carriers by describing the integrated sessions as a "love-in". Perhaps I might quote from a special bulletin issued on May 16 by the LCUC to its membership. It reads:
The Letter Carriers' Union of Canada has no animosity or dislike for our brothers and sisters in the Canadian Union of Postal Workers because, being trade unionists, we certainly should be able to find more in common than in opposition.
I do not intend to become involved in a paper war with CUPW and have more important issues to resolve for workers than to engage in a fight over false bulletins published by CUPW. I do, however, feel that our members, who are unaware of the facts, deserve to read them from their union.
The LCUC has been insulted by various CUPW officers for participating in the problem-solving consultation program, which has proven successful in resolving issues for our members. The CUPW referred to these meetings as "love-ins" and other insulting names in an attempt to downgrade our union and the national executive, realizing that names and insults evolve only from ignorance, agreed to allow the CUPW members to attend. We respected their refusal to participate in problem-solving and merely wanted to give them the opportunity to observe the program so that they could converse or criticize from a knowledgeable position. For this, our union has been condemned.
Then the bulletin goes on to state what happened. In fact, the integrated sessions both in Vancouver and in Halifax were picketed by CUPW because CUPW felt that those sessions might be threatening the legitimacy, in this particular context, of its adversarial stance. So when hon. members opposite criticize the Post Office for being insensitive to what is happening within the Post Office in this area, I cite the progress which is being made according to the testimony of one of the
Post Office
most militant groups in the Post Office, namely, the letter carriers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: I mentioned that in my speech.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for doing so. There is now some pressure on CUPW by virtue of the fact that these integrated sessions are proving successful. This is why I looked upon the telegram today as an indication of their intention to suspend negotiations, to see whether there could not be a similar sort of problem-solving arrangement in their province. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris quoted me, flatteringly, as having said that the Post Office was at a very crucial stage. This is not because I am at the helm. It is because of a series of factors.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: The Post Office has other problems besides you.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
I recognize that, in all due humility. I am a very modest person. When we look at the history of the Post Office, we find that at one time in Canada the Post Office was the only means of communication in the country, the only means of communicating at a distance. Initially, we used the canoe, and then we used the ox-cart before progressing to the pony express. I hear they still use these in Brandon-Souris. Later we proceeded to use the railways and aircraft. But all the time we were progressing in terms of transportation modes we were facing increased competition, competition in the form of improved technology. Some of the problems the Post Office now faces are the result of the success story represented by the Canadian communications industry. We in Canada have one of the most sophisticated telecommunications networks in the world. Yesterday my eldest child was asking me whether it was true that Canada had launched satellites. I said yes, we were third in importance in terms of satellites being launched in the world. Indeed, we have the best satellite communications system in the world. This is one of the direct reasons we have lost a great deal of business in the Post Office, as well as losing some credibility.
The advent of telecommunications has raised the expectations of Canadians in terms of instantaneous communication. No matter how we use transportation systems which work faster and faster, we can never compete with instantaneous communications over wire, over microwave, and over Telesat or satellite. As a result of that, the telephone, telex and other systems have removed a great deal of business from our particular operation.
When we look at the nature of the business that comes through the Post Office today, Mr. Speaker, we see that 80 per cent of the first-class mail is business mail originating from institutions, from government, from business or other organizations. Only 20 per cent is personal mail. Although that represents an increase from 2.5 billion to 3 billion pieces, it puts us in a very vulnerable position since we have noticed that the progress we have made in telecommunications has resulted
5774

May 18, 1977
Post Office
in very little intracompany, intramural mail being sent any more. Large corporations and medium-sized corporations, and even small-sized corporations are using telecommunications such as telex, the telephone and facsimile. So in effect what is happening, Mr. Speaker, is that the mail we are getting is mailed created by intercompany communications. We are dealing, as well, with a large increase in our volume because of a little plastic card known as a credit card-Chargex, Bank Americard, Master Charge. As a result, we calculate that about two billion pieces of our mail includes cheques and statements. This makes our business today more and more a kind of one crop affair.
We are now progressing toward what we call an electronic payments system. Most of us make our mortgage payments- those of us fortunate enough to have mortgages-through prior authorization with the bank. These amounts are deducted by the banks. This is done automatically without it going through the mails, so there is no need to mail that kind of communication any more, save and except the private transaction. The hon. member seems incredulous. What it has to do with increased mail, Mr. Speaker, is that we now have volumes of mail which are vulnerable to changes in technology. I have indicated that we have lost mail volume as a result of improvements in technology in Canada. The hon. member may acknowledge that he uses the telephone now, where previously one in his position would have used the mail. How many of his constituents call him, as opposed to sending him a letter through the mails? This is my point. We now have businesses which are not using the post because in a short period of time we are going to have an electronic payments system which will remove that kind of business from the Post Office. Therefore, this increases our vulnerability. At no time are we more vulnerable, Mr. Speaker, than when we have work stoppages, as the hon. gentleman very well knows.
Last month I received a flyer from an association of hospital pensioners. The government of Ontario was requesting them to authorize the provincial government to pay their cheques directly into their bank accounts in the event of a work interruption. This is where our difficulty lies. When there are work interruptions, we lose business. We are so sophisticated in terms of the use of electronics in order to communicate that lost business never comes back. Once it leaves us, it is very difficult for us to get it back.

speechtext:
Yes, but I point out to the hon. gentleman that although five billion pieces of mail a year have passed through the Post Office over the last four years, there has been no

dramatic increase in the volume of mail. We are trying to encourage a peaceful situation within the Post Office. We want to integrate the marketplace to a greater extent.
We consider there are two aspects to the Post Office. One is the aspect of public service. That is an aspect the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) really believes in since she represents a number of communities which would not get any service unless it was subsidized. She represents, basically, a number of small communities in her riding which would not benefit from any mail service if it were, let us say, in private hands, because, not being profitable, the service would not be available. So in effect she is sure to approve continuation of that particular subsidization. We also service a number of towns in my riding, small communities which do not generate revenue sufficient even to pay the salary of the postmistress or postmaster, much less pay for the rent, cost of glue on the stamps, and so on. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling) knows that most of the communities within his area are non-revenue producing in terms of net cost and net profit.
The second aspect of the Post Office is in terms of our being a commercial institution. The Post Office is central to the marketplace. We have always been central to the marketplace. We are trying to a larger extent to integrate the marketplace and provide a better, more reliable and more efficient service. That is one reason we mechanized our operation. We wanted to get an increase in volume from the marketplace. We wanted to be in the position to offer better service and a wider variety of products. Unfortunately, there, again, we face very serious competition from the private sector, not in traditional services but in new services which have been created as a result of higher expectations and greater demands on the marketplace.
People tell me that we are losing business to courier post services. I agree that we have lost a great deal of business to the private carriers. The couriers are now conducting an operation in which the Post Office has never engaged, namely, pick-up and delivery with limited volume handling in between. That has never been something which the Post Office has engaged in, but we are now seriously looking at that particular market. As I said last November, this is one area the Post Office should get into.
Next, we are facing competition in the handling of parcel post, our parcel or fourth-class mail operation. In 1973-74 we dealt with about 76 million pieces. In 1974-75 we dealt with 73 million pieces. In 1975-76 we dealt with 62 million pieces. So our volumes are going down, and they are going down because of the competition we are facing from the private sector. This is why I was a little uptight at the comment made by the hon. member from Winnipeg who objected to our using postpak in order to meet competition in parcel post. Postpak is a profitmaking product which we are offering to the marketplace and which we are able to handle.

Whether we like it or not, we are dealing with an operation which is massive in scope. We have 8,600 postal installations

in Canada, we have 60,000 employees, and we are dealing with about 12,000 letter carrier walks. You cannot get rid of that tomorrow; you cannot say, "Zap, you are gone".

Those things need directives and political will to put them in place. They will be put in place in the event no other service is available.
The effect of a long strike, such as the 42-day strike we had in 1975, will have that consequence. It will put that technology in place and further destroy the Post Office as a viable institution. I would ask hon. gentlemen to put their minds to that problem and try to persuade many of the people in the Post Office and management whom they may know that there has to be flexibility and an acceptable attitude on the part of all. I am not talking about money here, because hon. members know there are severe restrictions under the Anti-Inflation Board. Mr. Speaker, we always walk into that one; there is always somebody else to blame. Why do we not accept responsibility for some of the failures of
May 18, 1977

our own services? In this general connection, I was delighted with the appointment of the Lambert commission to examine accountability in the public service. It may be able to put its finger on the problems and the necessity of accountability. This brings me to the point made by the new chairman of the Public Service Commission when speaking to the International Personnel Management Association in Ottawa on November 17, 1976. It is distressing to me, as a former public servant, to have to agree in large measure with Mr. Gallant when he said:
Let me turn now to another general area of concern: the pervasive malaise which seems to affect Canada's public service today. We are all sensing that some public servants are losing their sense of purpose, that some have difficulty in strengthening or maintaining their sense of loyalty, that some find it increasingly difficult to understand the ideals, goals and objectives they are expected to uphold and pursue.
I am not directing those remarks to any part of the public service, but it is true, unfortunately, that this malaise does pervade our public service. Somehow or other we have lost the contact between those who serve and those who are being served. Later in his address, Mr. Gallant said:
The process of personnel management is shared by a number of authorities: The Treasury Board secretariat, the Public Service Commission, the Privy Council office, deputy heads of departments and their managers, and the various public service unions and staff associations. Each of these partners is charged with specific responsibilities and has commensurate powers to carry out such responsibilities. As long as all partners are operating within the same policy context, the process has a chance to work reasonably well. Vibrations throughout the public service today give rise to questions as to whether we still have in the daily decisions of these many partners, the degree of harmony which is necessary for the system to work satisfactorily.
This is a general comment about the public service as a whole. I know that those who are in it, feel it. We dealt with this over a year ago in the special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service, and I shall come back to that matter. I want to focus more closely on the Post Office for a moment, and I think it is worth recording a few statistics for that purpose.
I think I am correct in saying the largest single union in the public service is CUPW, with 23,000 of the 320,000 public servants as members. There are 16,500 members in the Letter Carriers Union, 8,200 members in the Canadian Postal Association, and 3,600 in the Association of Postal Officials of Canada. So we are dealing with over 50,000 employees, or about one-sixth of the public service. It is a very important segment, and one that performs a service which the Canadian public expects to receive and is paying for. I think it is important, in this context, to recognize the strike danger which is hanging over the heads of the Canadian people like the sword of Damocles. A public stance has been taken by those entering negotiations to the effect that a strike is possible, so that sword will fall unless we dissipate the distrust and misunderstanding that bedevils relations between employer and employee in the Post Office, as elsewhere.
In these circumstances, it is not only important, but essential, I consider, that we press more and more strongly for the introduction of legislation flowing from the recommendations of the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service, usually called the Finkelman report. The report was submitted to the House on February
Post Office
26, 1976. We are now in the month of May, 1977, and there have been no results arising from the report.
It is not necessary to remind the Postmaster General of the care with which we all dealt with the submissions made to that committee, because before becoming Postmaster General he was a member of that committee and a faithful attender at its meetings. Those of us who were there will testify that he was there in earnest and he shared in the formulation of the recommendations. There are some matters, however, which need to be mentioned just to underline their importance in the public service context. I think it would be worth-while now, 15 or 16 months after that report was tabled in the House, to select some of the recommendations of that committee and cite them to show how directly they are related to the unease in the Post Office.
We will not all agree with these recommendations. We do not all agree that they have to be implemented in their entirety, nor will all the recommendations agree with the very thoughtful presentation made to the committee by the Canadian Union of Postal Workers. However, that is not the point. The point is that from those recommendations a number of legislative measures ought to flow, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I propose to cite some of these recommendations so that we can be reminded just how important they are in the present context. The very first one is reminiscent of the motion we have before us. It reads as follows:
That a special task force be established to review the Public Service Employment Act and the role of the commission in personnel management and employer-employee relations in the public service-
The recommendation in the motion of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) is that a special joint committee be set up. That is a slight variation of the recommendation I just cited. I do not wish to cite all the recommendations. There are 72 in all and they are all worth reading. However, I am going to select a few in order to indicate how they bear on the situation with respect to the Post Office. Recommendation No. 8 reads as follows:
That there is a need for additional procedural and substantive amendments to the law governing the collective bargaining relationship, and more appropriate remedies for unlawful activity.
We have heard about unlawful activity. These are matters which ought to be considered very carefully by this House. Recommendation No. 15 reads:
That the Public Service Staff Relations Act be amended to require the designation of all employees whose functions involve the provision of services which in accordance with this act are to be provided without interruption.
There is not general agreement on that recommendation, and I am not suggesting there is, but some legislative provisions containing the substance of it ought to be before us so we can examine them and see whether we can accept them in the form in which they are presented. Why do we have to wait so long for that legislation? Recommendation No. 16 reads:
That the bargaining agents and the employers continue to be required to determine, by agreement, the employees in the bargaining units who are to be designated.

This matter of designation was a very important point in the submission which was put forward by CUPW when it presented its brief to us a year and a half or two years ago. Recommendation No. 34 reads this way:
That, having regard to the established jurisdiction of bargaining agents in the public service, bargaining classification standards be interpreted to mean the determination of the relative worth of jobs within an occupational group.
That is a complicated recommendation. We studied the matter very carefully, and that recommendation was the result. Recommendation No. 35 reads:
That provision be made in the law for the bargaining of classification standards following the three-year period after promulgation.
Again, there will not be general agreement with the actual terms of that, but it has to be discussed here and in committee. Why do we have to continue to wait? Recommendation No. 39 reads:
That resort to strike or lock-out to resolve classification disputes be prohibited.
Again there is going to be argument. That is what this House is for. Recommendation No. 41 reads:
That classification grievances which are not resolved in the grievance process should be referrable to adjudication.
All these matters were raised in the CUPW submission. Recommendation No. 42 deals with a matter which is at the core of the present problem. It reads as follows:
That changes in technology, operations, organization or any other dimension of the structure or character of the employer's resources to provide service to the public be recognized as a prerogative of the employer.
That is going to cause argument. Fair enough. Then recommendation No. 43:
That the employer be obliged to bargain the impact of adverse changes on employees which may occur as a consequence of the employer's actions referred to in recommendation 42 above, including the advance notice of such changes and the details to accompany the notice.
These are the matters which are causing our postal workers concern. Decisions are made and implemented, and the worker is faced with them without any consultation whatever. This recommendation underlines the need for consultation before implementation. 1 would like to cite one more recommendation, No. 65, as follows:
That where a bargaining agent conducts a strike vote, or submits a proposal for a collective agreement to its membership for approval,
(a)	The vote should be carried out by secret ballot in accordance with procedures prescribed by regulations of the Public Service Staff Relations Board; and
(b)	A breach of the regulations of the board in this respect should constitute a contravention of the Act, and the union or persons concerned should be subject to the appropriate penalties-
Those are important recommendations, and I am at a loss to understand why we should be delayed so long in seeing the legislation we expected to flow from them. There are other recommendations concerning pay research and casuals. I do not need to cite any more because I think the ones I have cited make it amply clear how important these recommendations are and how essential, in the present context, a bill containing these recommendations in legal form would be.

I think we all recognize that there is a growing desire in Canada to remove the ability to strike from the public service or from parts of the public service designated as essential. This desire is growing because of the number of strikes there have been in the public service. The Postmaster General said that during a strike the Post Office loses some of the business it had previously and never gets it back. The only way to combat this is to make proper provision, under the law, for grievances.
We went through this exercise in committee, and a crippling strike or two could build pressure for the removal of that ability which those contemplating a strike ought to bear in mind. I have heard rumblings suggesting that a strike may not be far off. A strike is a distinct possibility, if news reports are to be believed. 1 hope they are not to be believed. Therefore, action is demanded. What action should be taken? First, we should establish a joint committee as proposed in the motion of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) referred to certain studies, but is of the opinion that further studies are not important. Certain studies were undertaken in the past, but the findings were neither revealed nor released. I say such studies ought to be available to the special committee.
Second, we need to introduce the sort of legislation which ought to have flowed from the Finkelman report. Such legislation could assist in the resolution of the problems of the Post Office and would apply throughout the public service. I ask, when will the government take either one, or both, actions to which I have just alluded?

The national service has improved correspondingly. I hope the improvement continues. Canada Post is confident that postal service will continue to improve as Toronto overcomes its
May 18, 1977

initial problems. The ultimate success in rebuilding a first-rate postal system will depend on the degree to which this massive mechanized system can be utilized. This, in turn, depends directly on the widespread use of the postal code which Canada Post urges all postal users to promote.
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) recently made statements to the effect that the Post Office cannot survive unless its situation improves drastically. The time has come for everyone, in the public and private sectors alike, to work together to improve our postal system. Let us stop blaming one another for the difficult and tense situation that exists at the Post Office and do everything in our power to restore its image. Canada as a whole will be the better for it.
During the next few minutes I will attempt to give the House an outline of two ideas that have been suggested to improve Canadian postal service. Certain people maintain that postal service would improve if the Canada Post Office were to become a Crown corporation. The postal administrations of Germany, Great Britain and the United States have become independent organizations, yet their problems seem to be getting worse and worse. Some critics have what they consider to be the definitive answer to what they see as government bungling in the Post Office: hand the whole thing over to private enterprise. These people will be pleased to know that this, exactly, is going on. The only difference is that the assimilation is a gradual one as private courier services proliferate.
Are those companies really more efficient? Some are; some are not. Their prices and operating costs are much higher than those of the Post Office. They deliver only within or between large cities, where costs are low and profits enormous, and they generously concede the Post Office the right to pick up and deliver parcels in the isolated regions of Newfoundland, in small towns, in crossroads stores and in Arctic settlements. The private courier, of course, measures efficiency by the dollar. He expands only when profitable. He spends only to make more. His only aim-a perfectly laudable one-is to make a buck. But the Post Office has another mandate: to serve, to bind, to unite, to provide a communications web that links Canadians wherever they live. This means that every farmer and every villager can pay his 12 cents and plug into a nationwide communications network-820 domestic air flights, 7,639 contract truck routes, 90 freight and passenger trains, and 12,520 letter carrier routes; and, for a few cents more, you have a choice of 110 international flights to almost every country in the world.
On the day that private enterprise wants to take over this job, on the day it guarantees to deliver mail of all types and sizes to every place in Canada as quickly and as cheaply as the Post Office does, then will be the time to agree with its critics: let them do it. In the meantime, the private couriers are skimming the profitable cream and leaving the Post Office and the public the rest. The Post Office deficit for the last fiscal year soared to $546 million, or $225 million more than for the previous year. Yet a great number of people nostalgically
Post Office
recall the "good old days" when all you had to do was affix a four-cent stamp on a letter and the letter carrier delivered twice-a-day letters which had often been mailed the previous night. As Oscar Wilde once said, the charm of the past is that it is past. The letter carrier no longer appears at your doorstep twice a day, for the same reason that the baker no longer delivers once a day. Gone forever is the era of the four-cent stamp, of the five-cent cup of coffee and of dialling "Ma Bell" to get the correct time. Trains no longer stop in every small town to pick up passengers, just as the sorting of mail is no longer done aboard trains. The Post Office has changed, because nothing is as it was.
In a manner of speaking, the Post Office was a victim of its own success. Cities grew and prospered. Businesses of all kinds expanded, the flow of mail increased, transportation was revolutionized, the public service recognized the rights of unions, and postal service began to lag behind. The Post Office had to move quickly to ensure that the Canadian postal service continued to meet the needs of the population. In addition to other pressing matters, the situation is further complicated by a lack which has preoccupied Post Office communicators a great deal. Somewhere along the way the lines of communication between management and employees seem to have broken down. How can we remedy this situation? One thing that was done a short time ago was to have a National Film Board crew, headed by a sociologist from the University of Alberta, interview rank and file employees at mechanized installations in Vancouver, Saint John, New Brunswick, and Winnipeg. The interviews were extremely revealing and extremely valuable as a management tool. It was found that the average employee's chief complaint is that he feels like the invisible man, working in an environment where his views are neither solicited nor considered by management, that mechanization is being introduced without regard to its effect on his future in the Post Office.

speechtext:
Obviously, it is imperative that some way be found to get their views on the post office. The mechanization program is important to the increased efficiency that the Post Office must achieve if it is to survive. But it will not work without people. Many of those who work for the Post Office believe it has entered a crisis stage in its long and proud history of service to the people of Canada, a crisis which could be termed one of productivity. This crisis is not exclusive to Canada. It is a serious and almost insoluble problem faced by all postal administrations of the industrialized nations of the free world. Chief among the approaches to its problems, the Post Office is looking to automation for a solution; it is replacing men with machines. The young worker now enters the scene, he is better educated, anxious to prove himself and

May 18, 1977
Post Office
to make a contribution to the organization. He finds it boring to do repetitive tasks. His work is dull and unrewarding. He feels that he is contributing nothing. But what is the solution? Is there, in fact, a solution to this problem? Can the Post Office survive under its present form? Automation can work if workers want it to, and I do not think that professional ethics are dead.
More and more, the Post Office is attempting to ensure the development of its employees as well as that of the postal system. Nowadays, the aspirations of employees seeking development and satisfaction in the job is taken into consideration. Attempts are being made to stimulate their enthusiasm. But this was not always the case. Unfortunately, for a long time Post Office workers were treated as if they were consumer goods and not members of a team. Management let the search for efficiency take over, and employees could not help but think the employer was more interested in the system than in them. But in spite of all that, thousands of workers remain proud of the job they have.
All that the Post Office management has learned in the past few years points clearly to the need for a change in attitude of both union and management. The two sides must find a way to back off from the adversary stance that each has adopted in the past. Only in this way will mutual co-operation, improved employee morale and increase productivity and efficiency be achieved. It is apparent that a mixed participation in the decision-making process could solve most of the labour problems. The challenge is not an easy one.
