speechtext:
This is so of all levels, from the top to the bottom. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was in Europe

preening himself before the television cameras which were compelled to go over there to watch him, I wonder if he thought about the Post Office and how it was degenerating, going underground more and more. He does not worry. The Prime Minister is one of the principal architects of the disunity of this country, the man who created the legion of the condemned of one million unemployed, the man who was going to wrestle inflation to the ground.
These issues are summed up in what is the difficulty with the Post Office, a once proud institution, dependable, reliable, resourceful, with a good relationship between management and employees and between the institution and the public. That has vanished. Will it come back? I do not know. However, this is prevalent to a greater or lesser degree in every institution of the government of Canada today. There have been many causes. Obviously, staring us in the face is incompetence and maladministration. With due respect to the minister-and I give him the benefit of this doubt-there have been far too many ministers over the past 15 or 18 years that I can recall. When there is a man to be placed somewhere, they either make him minister without portfolio or postmaster general. The hon. member for Crowfoot, now the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Horner), lost in that one. He is the Minister without Portfolio. Whether the Post Office is the beneficiary of that situation, I do not know.
The ministers are there so briefly they become agents and spokesmen for their senior officials. That is what happens. It happens with too many ministers, for a number of reasons. Parliament is being abandoned as a result of the attitude taken by the Prime Minister. It trickles down by a form of intellectual cosmosis, if the word "intellectual" can be applied to this government. It simply disregards this institution.
One of the reasons for the problems which confront us today is the government's arrogance and attempts to bypass this parliament as often as possible. That is part of the motion which the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) put before this House today and which the minister and the parliamentary secretary have been unwilling to answer. I want to deal with that, if I have time, because it is a very simple indication of what causes the problems to the Post Office and to so many other departments of government.
Just a few days ago, the Standing Joint Committee on Statutory and Other Instruments brought in a unanimous report which condemned the Post Office and, by inference, charged the Post Office with engaging in illegal action by increasing the rate for first-class mail without obtaining approval from parliament. The case was documented faithfully and well. I sat on that committee. It was not a partisan issue at all, as I am not being partisan now. What I say will, I hope, be listened to by hon. members opposite.
The facts which were admitted and the facts which were proved by the committee as the basis for its report are an indication of what troubles us today. We pointed out in that report, which was tabled and is now available for discussion,
May 18, 1977

that on May 21, 1976, the then postmaster general, Mr. Mackasey, stated he was not going to proceed by way of legislation but by order in council under section 13B of the Financial Administration Act. Mr. Speaker, from time immemorial postage rates have been an issue affecting the average person in this country, just as tax rates do. Yet the government has seen fit to take this surreptitious means of avoiding the kind of discussion which should go on in this chamber by raising the rates without coming to parliament and by attempting to rely on the Financial Administration Act.
I have read that act. I was involved in the debate on the amendment when section 13 was brought in in its present form. There was only a passing reference from the President of the Treasury Board to this issue. It was never intended or expected that the Postmaster General, for instance, at the instigation of his officials, would be able to bypass parliament and change first-class mail rates in this way.
Section 6 of the Post Office Act makes the matter plain. It says that the Postmaster General can make regulations for the official operation of the Post Office and that he can fix rates of postage on mail for delivery outside Canada. By that legislation, as it was amended, the Post Office Act fixes the rate for first-class mail. I submit there is very grave doubt as to whether what the government has done is legal. It is certainly improper. It had the result of prohibiting the type of discussion which should take place in this chamber where the people are represented. Surely, an issue which affects so many million Canadians should be discussed here. We might have agreed with the Postmaster General that he had a good case for raising the rates. But I deplore the attempt by bureaucrats to push this institution to one side and carry out these acts by orders in council in the depth of secrecy.

speechtext:
We talk about secrecy. Secrecy is mentioned in the motion. There were two reports, the Hays report and the Mulligan report. My hon. friend from Brandon-Souris request-
Post Office
ed the production of these documents. This was refused on the ground that they were internal working papers. Mr. Speaker, if they were working papers containing advice and opinions, there might be good reason for not producing them. But if they were documents, as I understand they were, containing a large quantity of factual and statistical material together with recommendations with regard to certain changes, it is not only the duty of the government to make them available to the House for discussion, but it is the government's responsibility to do so, as it is our responsibility to demand them. It is only through argument, discussion and proposals for change that we make this country work. A government working in secrecy, denying itself the opportunity of hearing the views of the representatives of the people will inevitably get into difficulty.
I am told by my hon. friend from Brandon-Souris that he was invited to go over with other members to see those documents privately. I am glad he refused such a proposal. It is unthinkable that an hon. member representing, as he does, the official opposition and charged with a particular responsibility in connection with the Post Office, should be invited to examine these documents in private and later find himself unable to speak about them. My hon. friend showed good character and strong judgment in not accepting this offer.
I have here a copy of a letter which appeared in the Globe and Mail of March 31, 1976, over the signature of Frank E. Thomas of Willowdale, Ontario. It reads:
In spite of all that's been said about the federal government for secrecy, it's not abating. On the contrary, it seems to have afflicted a department one would not have suspected of such practices.
On March 25 I asked a clerk in the Fairview Mall, Willowdale, post office, for a copy of the current postal rates. The answer was: "We haven't received them yet.'' When I inquired if another rate change had just occurred, I learned that the one effective last January 1 was still in effect.
On March 26 I made the same request in station B (Bayview Village shopping centre) and was advised that copies of postal rates were not available. When I asked where I might get a copy, I was told, "You'll have to go to Ottawa for it."
I cannot afford to go to Ottawa. And even if I could, I doubt that the Post Office there would let me have a copy since it seems determined to withhold them from the general public.
Perhaps the Globe and Mail's Ottawa bureau, which seems to have been able to obtain other confidential government publications, could excel itself and get a copy of this evidently ultra-secret document, for publication in an early issue.
For an ordinary citizen of this country to go to the post office and to ask for a copy of the current postal rates, and then to be contemptuously told to go to Ottawa to obtain this material, is a terrible situation. So long as that kind of situation prevails, Mr. Speaker, the Post Office is going to be in trouble and the country is going to be in trouble.
I suggest that instead of the minister coming here and indicting civilization, which seems to be the basis of his defence of the Post Office-hq accuses progress in the world of taking away from his organization the business to which it is entitled, which is a scathing indictment of technological improvement and scientific change in this country-he should be more honest, open and candid with this House. Let him lay first before the committee, and ultimately before this House,
5782

May 18, 1977
Post Office
the problems which confront him. Let this House into the arena, so it can help. It can only do this if it is made aware of the facts. If this happens, Mr. Speaker, hopefully we can look forward to some improvement in the situation. But it will not happen until this government tears away the veil of secrecy and learns through this parliament that the people of Canada are at least entitled to be junior partners in the business of government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Milne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to enter the debate not so much to either oppose or support the motion which has been put forward by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), but more particularly because of the importance of the mail service in the Toronto area, the volume that goes through there and the difficulty which has been experienced with the Gateway facility. I happen, along with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott), to represent ridings which surround the Gateway facility and we have been involved in this issue for quite some considerable time. I thought I would like to put a few comments on the record relating to the history of this facility and to where I think the mail service in the Toronto area may well be headed.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to defend the decision taken by the government and by the Post Office some time ago to move to three large automated facilities in the Toronto area. It has not been easy to live with the consequences of that decision while the facilities are being introduced, people are being moved and the new machinery is being started up. Probably it would have been much easier for people who are dependent on the mails, and for members of parliament to service constituency problems, if it had not occurred at this point in time. On the other hand, I think it is important that the Post Office do keep abreast of modern technology and make this decision. One has only to look at some of the deplorable postal situations in some European countries which did not keep abreast of technology and allowed the old system to prevail to the point where, as I recall from reading some articles, they simply destroyed large amounts of mail to dispose of it.
In the Toronto area, very close to 50 per cent of all mail in Canada is handled daily in these three facilities. Of those three facilities, I would judge a large percentage, 45 per cent, goes through the Gateway facility at the west end of Toronto. While the point has been made by a number of speakers today that the mail in total is not increasing at an alarming rate, certainly the amount of mail in the Toronto area is increasing, and the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) said that this is because of the growth in the business community in that area. The high percentage of mail originating from and directed to businesses means that in the Toronto area, certainly in my opinion, the Post Office Department was correct to move to a highly automated facility.
My major criticism would be that this decision should have been taken earlier. There should have been more time to implement this change. Perhaps one of the real difficulties with which the postal people in the Toronto area have been

working has been to try to institute the amount of change which is required within such a short period of time. I think that in fairness hon. members should appreciate just what has had to happen in the Toronto area in this regard. Post offices in the Toronto area have been transferred to these three facilities at the same time as the mail has had to be kept moving. If this were a private organization manufacturing a product, I suggest that the company would have built up its inventory to a very large level and then used the inventory to service its customers while shutting down its one plant and starting up its new facility. But the Post Office could not do that; they had to introduce the new facility, new machinery and procedures, at the same time handling the mail on a daily basis.
This could be likened to Ford or General Motors shutting down their major factory and moving to a new location, with no inventory and not missing any production. In this respect I think we should appreciate the enormity of what has been undertaken in the last two years in the Toronto area, particularly in the last 18 months. These three large postal facilities have had to deal with equipment which had never been either used or designed prior to its introduction. It was prototype machinery which had to be designed specifically and on a scale to do functions which had never been automated before. While I suppose a number of start-up problems were anticipated, I do not think that anyone, particularly the Post Office and perhaps the designers of the equipment, ever anticipated the amount of trouble they have had in terms of start-up.
I make that point because not only has it affected very drastically the mail service in the constituency that I represent just north of the Gateway facility, but it has also affected mail service across Canada, since so much of the mail passes through the facility. I think the hon. member who introduced the motion would agree that it has only been in the last ten days or two weeks that intercity mail passing through Gateway has started to move at the efficiency that we want and should expect.
Another matter which I should like to put on the record is that most of the systems within the Gateway facility have been installed and are now in operation. I hope that all hon. members can come to the Gateway facility and tour it. It is an enormous area, about the size of four football fields. You need a guide to take you around because you might not find your way out, it is almost that extensive. When the mail comes in, it goes into a pre-sorting area, and right from the first that facility has worked well. It then goes to the colour phaser canceller, as they call it, and this facility has also worked relatively well. The biggest problem has been that the mail goes from there on to trays which move forward on a computer program for sorting. This has been a real problem in terms of introducing the facility and getting acceptable mail service at Gateway.
These trays were manufactured by one of the largest companies operating in Canada, the name of which is well known to
May 18, 1977

everyone in this House. The plastic composition of the material which was used in them was apparently not correct. It was very brittle. The trays were very, very marginally manufactured too large. As a result, there was a good deal of jamming in the automatic guides. When the trays would jam, they would break.
The Post Office at Gateway has fought this problem for about a year. They finally reached agreement with the supplier as to liability and an agreement was arranged whereby these trays would have to be replaced. There has been some hold-up on that, but I am advised the problem is now being solved. That complete section of the service should go on stream or under test July 1. If that is so, and if it is successful at that date, the Gateway facility will start to operate in the manner in which it was designed. Some two or three weeks ago, I am advised, the last phase was set up for the handling of off-size envelopes and the parcel operation. The many different things which had to be produced there are now all operating. The continuing problem with these trays and the automated computer program associated with it is in the process of being solved.
The problem which was there in terms of personnel should not be underestimated. The theory of these large postal installations in the Toronto area was to transfer functions, which were being carried out in a large number of small post offices, to these big three. Not everyone wanted to follow the transfer of those functions. Many employees chose not to continue to work for the Post Office and commute longer distances. Thus, there had to be many new people hired. The hiring of people was not the problem. It was training and finding enough new supervisors to get the system into operation. That has been largely overcome, and very successful.
Some rather critical comments about Post Office employees and their unions have been raised by previous speakers today. I do not intend to enter into that area because I think it has been sufficiently spoken to by other members. I would like to pay tribute to many of the people who work in the Post Office. Most of my constituents would join me in saying it is remarkable that as many people could be transferred as was the case with the start-up of the Gateway facility. There were a number of new procedures and concepts started there, and we have not had any major labour difficulty.
I do not want to be quoted too tightly on this, but it could well be the union might have a case for argument if they followed the small letter of their contract in terms of automation and the introduction of it. I want to congratulate the unions because they took a bigger view and realized what was required, which was an open attitude involving as much assistance as possible in getting the facility to worK. When people are being critical of the postal staff, they should appreciate that nearly all the people in the Toronto area who are handling almost half of Canada's mail have had their place of work transferred. Many of them are now working under new procedures and with new machines. This has been accomplished without a major problem, and that is a tribute to them.
Post Office
I would like to say a word about many of my friends who deliver mail door to door. There is no question there have been problems in the Post Office about the level of service. Most people complain to the letter carriers. It is not their fault. They have been good ambassadors for the Post Office and we should be appreciative of them. In making those comments, I am not saying all is, or has been, well in the Toronto area in terms of the postal service. I have spent a good deal of time meeting with management at Gateway and dealing with this problem. I have had many letters from my constituents. I have had strong representations from the Brampton Board of Trade and from many individual businessmen. Many of these businessmen have lost substantial amounts of money because they submitted tenders which arrived late and were not accepted. This has been difficult. It had to happen some time during this automation phase in order to handle increased volumes of mail at reasonable cost in future years.
Some six weeks ago I was hopeful because Gateway was up to a point where there was almost 80 per cent of next day delivery. Then two things happened: there was a four-day Easter weekend, and because of the contract with the employees the facility was essentially closed for that time, which generated a tremendous backlog of mail. Then having overcome that to a degree, some of the feed-in mail did not arrive on schedule because of start-up problems which were inherent in the facility on Eastern Avenue in the central core of Toronto. This facility is probably five or six weeks behind the one in Scarborough and the one in Gateway. While they are learning from experiences the other two have had, there are problems there. Many times we blame Gateway, and it is not Gateway's fault. It is just the fact that the mail coming from the core of the city has not reached Gateway and, therefore, letters from downtown Toronto to my constituency are delayed at that facility rather than at Gateway.
There is light at the end of the tunnel. During the last ten days all the mail at Gateway has been sorted and cleared from the facility by 6.30 in the morning. The manager and supervisory staff at Gateway have worked hard. They have been working 18 hours a day. They come in very early in the morning, go out on the floor and look at each of the systems. They make sure any problems are looked after and that the mail is moving through the system. It is encouraging to note the mail has been coming in on schedule, is being processed, sorted and sent back out by 6.30 in the morning for ten consecutive days. This indicates that many of the inherent problems are being solved.
By July 1, when the problems in the downtown facility on Eastern Avenue are cleared up and this automated tray process has been corrected, the kind of mail service we expect, and should have as a result of the expenditure in Gateway, should be forthcoming. No one hopes more than I do that it will be improved. I doubt very many members of the House of Commons have as many constituents who are concerned and upset with the level of service as I have. One exception might be my hon. friend, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate
80016-26^2

May 18, 197'
Post Office
Affairs, representing the Mississauga riding. I hope these problems are under control, and I expect they may well be.
It is encouraging to look at the facilities in western Canada, where the same type of automated service has been installed and brought on stream. It demonstrates that this system improves efficiency and mail service. I am talking now about most of the facilities in western Canada. It has demonstrated that the system does improve the efficiency of the mail service. The concept is correct, but the biggest problem has been the mechanical aspect of it and getting this new, highly-automated equipment to work.
I should like to make three points in closing, if I may, Mr. Speaker. While we complain about the mail service, there have been some good things about it and I think we should compliment the Post Office on those and put them on the record. Members on all sides of the House have been fairly strong in expressing the opinion that government should exercise restraint of government spending. In major statements to the House, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) have given the commitment that government spending will be controlled and, parallel to that, that the growth of the public service will be virtually frozen. In this fiscal year I believe the growth will be less than 1 per cent. While we all applaud that, we have to understand the position of fast growing areas of the country.
I represent a constituency where the population is growing faster than any other area of Canada. That means new streets almost daily. When people move in, there is a problem supplying them with door to door service, when at the same time there is a freeze on hiring additional delivery men. This problem has been handled well by the Post Office. Certainly, many people in my riding have had to wait for door to door delivery; some have been patient and others have made representations to which I have tried to respond.
By virtue of using small vehicles to take mail out to the routes, the same number of men can deliver to more houses than before. They spend less time waiting for lifts to the post office to get more mail or waiting for public transportation. I think we should compliment those men. It is conceivable that the system would be opposed by door to door delivery men because they are being asked to service more doors; but, instead, they have done it well. It has meant that the same number of door to door delivery men in many areas of high growth have been able to deliver mail to a good many more new residents than would have been the case under the old system. I think we should be positive about that.
[Mr. Milne.)
Mr. Speaker, I see my time is running out. I have two more very brief points, and if the House agrees I shall put them on the record very quickly. I leave it to the Chair to ask whether there is consent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
I will be brief, Mr. Speaker. While we complain about the Post Office, I think there is a responsibility on us to look at how we prepare mail by use of the postal code, appropriate envelopes, and so on. Having installed a lot of automated equipment, there is real concern about the low percentage of mail that can be treated automatically.
I want to go on record as supporting the Postmaster General. I think we should be very vigorous in competing for the entire mail service. We should be in the courier business because it is the responsibility of the Post Office to service all areas. This is not an argument about public or private service; this is a matter of being involved in things that are profitable and will bring down the cost that we have to bear if we are to bring this service to all Canadians, as is their right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last debate on the Post Office I believe Your Honour was in the chair. I was called on then just three minutes before the time expired, and I see today that I have an extra minute. As a member of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, I have been critical of the Post Office Department. I know that my colleague and neighbour in Nipissing, the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) has great problems to face.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne) about the Gateway facilities being the size of four football fields. I thought they were the size of one football field, but I understand now they are the size of four. 1 was going to speak about slow delivery and various other things, but in my view, Mr. Speaker, the fault with the Post Office is demonstrated by what I have seen here this afternoon. I look in the gallery and see those great officials of the Post Office, and I commend them for being here. Then I look to the far end and there is the great czar of CUPW, Joe Davidson and one of his henchmen. The two parties are as far apart as possible. Why could both parties not have been sitting closer together? I think this is most important.
It was mentioned earlier that everything would be all right by July 1, but then the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe said we might be in a tough spot by July 1. If we are, it will have nothing to do with the machinery or debugging it; what we have to debug is the adversary system that exists between


May 18, 1977

management and the workers. That is the crux of the whole thing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED INABILITY OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE EFFICIENT POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
I am not saying that one party is to blame more than the other; they are both guilty. Time and again I have said that the people of Canada want them to iron out their differences and get the mail delivered. They do not want a strike. To lay it on the line, they do no want them to be allowed to strike. That is it-one, two, three. I am sure that is unpopular with the union and others as well, but people are fed up with the mail service as it is. The adversary system is no good at all. They should get together. I mentioned this to the Postmaster General in committee. I said, "J.-J., you should sit down with Davidson and company"-and he is a human being; I hear that Scotch burl of his-"Highland Joe." My ancestors came from Scotland. I said, "He has a sense of humour, maybe distorted at times, but surely you can talk to these people as human beings. That is the secret. That is the only way you are going to avert a strike."
Post Office
My colleague, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), and I were in England recently investigating the post office there. I learned a lot, but one thing that amazed me was that the union, from the shop steward up to the top official who holds the same job as Joe Davidson, were sympathetic to management. They were proud of the post office and were aware of the competition they faced from couriers and various other organizations that were cutting into their revenue. They felt they had to stick together or sink together.
That is the message I want to get across to the Postmaster General and his cohorts, and to Davidson and his cohorts. It is as simple as that. Once we get that message across, we will not have to worry about automation and the rest of it. It will fit in, and it will be well oiled and greased.
